analysis.one_liner: Gives holdout states full federal funding to expand Medicaid coverage, whenever they choose to expand.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee vote or a House floor vote and died when the 116th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Under the Affordable Care Act, states could expand Medicaid to low-income adults, with the federal government covering most of the cost — 100% the first three years, then sliding down to 90%. But that deal was tied to calendar dates, so states that refused to expand early would get the lesser rate. This bill would give every state the full enhanced federal match based on how long it had been expanding, not when it started, and would apply retroactively. In practice, this was aimed at the roughly dozen states, including sponsor Rep. Veasey's Texas, that still had not expanded Medicaid.
analysis.who_benefits: Low-income uninsured adults in states that had not expanded Medicaid — mainly in the South — who could gain coverage if their state took the richer federal deal. State budgets in those states would also benefit, since Washington would pick up a larger share of the cost, and hospitals would see fewer unpaid bills.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Uninsured low-income adults in non-expansion states

how_it_helps.text: The bill gives every state that expands Medicaid the same enhanced federal match — 100% of costs for the first three years, 95% the fourth, 94% the fifth, 93% the sixth, and 90% after — counted from when the state starts, not from fixed calendar dates [S2][S3].
It applies retroactively, taking effect as if it had been part of the original Affordable Care Act, so a state expanding late would not be punished with a lower match [S2][S3].

For states that had held out — Texas, Florida, and others — this removed the main financial penalty for expanding late, making it cheaper to cover low-income adults who currently fall into a coverage gap [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers, who would fund the enhanced match — 90% or more of the cost of covering newly eligible adults — for every state that expands, including states that had refused for years. State governments in those states would still pay the remaining 10% share.

drawbacks.text: The bill increases federal spending: rewarding late-expanding states with the full 100%-to-90% match costs the federal government more than the 90% rate that applies under current law after the phase-down [S2][S3].
The retroactive, wait-and-you-get-the-full-deal design rewards states that held out longest, which critics of the ACA's original structure said weakens the incentive for states to act quickly [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The tradeoff is straightforward: more federal money in exchange for coverage for uninsured low-income adults in holdout states. The main honest objection is cost to the federal treasury and the awkwardness of rewarding states that declined for years — but the coverage gain for people in the Medicaid gap would have been substantial.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the Energy and Commerce Committee the day it was introduced, passed along to its Health Subcommittee a week later, and no committee or floor action ever followed before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Marc Veasey of Texas introduced the bill on January 16, 2019, with 15 original cosponsors [S1][S3].
It was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the same day [S5].
On January 25, 2019, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health, where it stayed [S5].
No hearing, markup, or floor vote ever occurred, and the bill died when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: State officials in non-expansion states who opposed expansion kept the status quo: their states never faced the richer federal offer, and federal spending on the Medicaid expansion stayed limited to the states that had already expanded. Hospitals and low-income adults in holdout states got nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Opponents of Medicaid expansion in holdout states

for.name: Rep. Marc Veasey
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to give late-expanding states the full federal Medicaid match; his state, Texas, was the largest holdout.

for.name: 39 of 231 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; every cosponsor was a Democrat and none was a Republican.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.role: Committee of referral (Chair: Rep. Frank Pallone, D-NJ)
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on January 16, 2019, sent it to the Health Subcommittee on January 25, and never took it up — no hearing, markup, or vote in two years.

sides.party_line_note: All 39 cosponsors plus the sponsor were Democrats; no Republican cosponsor appears in the record, and the Democratic-controlled committee never advanced the bill either.

industries.note: Hospitals in holdout states carry large uncompensated-care costs from uninsured patients; Medicaid expansion funded at 90%+ federal match would have relieved that. They are worse off because the bill died.
Insurers that run state Medicaid programs would have gained millions of new enrollees in holdout states. Their loss from the bill's death mirrors the public's loss of coverage.
These states would have received a far richer federal match than current law offers; refusing expansion left state residents uninsured and state budgets absorbing some care costs.
